events.title: Harappan art: seals, bronze and terracotta
events.summary: The Harappans make steatite seals with animals and script, the bronze "Dancing Girl" and the stone "Priest-King" of Mohenjodaro, red pottery painted in black, and terracotta figurines (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Harappan seal is the most distinctive artefact of the civilisation (NCERT); it usually carries an animal motif and a short line of script. One seal shows a figure seated cross-legged, surrounded by animals — called a "proto-Shiva" (NCERT). Beads were made of carnelian, jasper, crystal, faience and shell at Chanhudaro and Lothal (NCERT).

The bronze Dancing Girl was made by the lost-wax method. Other finds: the bearded "Priest-King" in steatite, the Great Bath and a dockyard at Lothal.
outcomes: Lost-wax bronze casting continued in India for 4,000 years.
facts: Seals were used for trade, as stamps on sealed goods (NCERT).
The Harappan script is not deciphered (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 1 "Bricks, Beads and Bones"

events.title: Early centres of learning: Taxila to Vikramashila
events.summary: Taxila (Takshashila) in Gandhara is a famous centre of learning by about 500 BCE; later come Nalanda (5th c.), Valabhi (Gujarat), Vikramashila and Odantapuri (Palas) — the "early educational institutions" of the syllabus.
events.detail:
Jataka stories tell of princes going to Taxila; by tradition Chanakya taught there and Panini and Charaka studied there. Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I; Xuanzang studied there. Valabhi was patronised by the Maitrakas; Vikramashila was founded by the Pala Dharmapala; Odantapuri by Gopala. In Andhra, Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati were great monastic centres.

Nalanda and Vikramashila were destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khalji (c. 1193–1203).
outcomes: Students came from China, Korea, Tibet and Southeast Asia.

alsoOn.text: Vikramashila founded by the Pala king Dharmapala.

events.yearHook: Taxila c. 500 BCE → Nalanda c. 427 CE → destroyed c. 1193.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Xuanzang was in India c. 630–643 CE.

events.title: Panini's Ashtadhyayi
events.summary: Panini of Gandhara composes the Ashtadhyayi (c. 5th–4th century BCE), a grammar of Sanskrit in about 4,000 short rules (sutras).
events.detail: It fixed the form of classical Sanskrit. Katyayana wrote notes (vartikas) on it and Patanjali the Mahabhashya (Shunga age) — the three "munis" of Sanskrit grammar.
outcomes: Classical Sanskrit standardised.
events.yearHook: Panini c. 400 BCE → Patanjali c. 150 BCE.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Other authors: Yajnavalkya (Smriti; Brihadaranyaka Upanishad), Kapila (Samkhya philosophy), Vatsyayana (Kamasutra), Shudraka (Mrichchhakatika), Dandin (Dashakumaracharita), Vasubandhu (Abhidharmakosha), Buddhaghosa (Visuddhimagga), Mahanama (Mahavamsa), Milinda Panha (Menander–Nagasena).

events.title: Mauryan art: Barabar caves and the Didarganj Yakshi
events.summary: Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha cut the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves in Bihar for the Ajivikas — India's oldest rock-cut caves; the polished Didarganj Yakshi and the pillar capitals show Mauryan court art.
events.detail: The Lomas Rishi cave has a carved doorway copying a wooden hut. The Mauryan polish gives a mirror-like shine to stone. Folk art includes the Yaksha and Yakshi figures of Parkham and Didarganj. Ashoka also built stupas over the Buddha's relics (NCERT).
outcomes: Start of rock-cut architecture in India.

participants.role: Stupas were built over his relics (NCERT).

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh); NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
facts: Mauryan art also includes the rock-cut elephant at Dhauli (Odisha), the Didarganj Yakshi (near Patna), the Great Stupa at Sanchi (begun by Ashoka) and the 80-pillared hall at Kumrahar (Pataliputra) (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Buddhist sites of Andhra: Guntupalli to Salihundam
events.summary: From about the 2nd century BCE Buddhist stupas, chaityas and viharas spread across Andhra: Guntupalli rock-cut chaitya (West Godavari), Salihundam, Sankaram, Bavikonda, Thotlakonda, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Bhattiprolu, Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda.
events.detail:
Guntupalli has a round rock-cut chaitya hall, one of the earliest in south India. Thotlakonda and Bavikonda near Visakhapatnam were sea-trade monasteries. Sankaram (Bojjannakonda) has rock-cut stupas. Ghantasala and Jaggayyapeta lay on the Krishna. Andhra Buddhism followed the Mahasanghika and later the Mahayana schools; Acharya Nagarjuna is linked with this land.

Jainism also had a presence in Andhra: Kharavela's patronage, and later Jaina centres such as Ramatirtham (Vizianagaram) and Danavulapadu (Kadapa).
outcomes: Andhra became a major centre of Buddhism for 800 years.
events.yearHook: 2nd century BCE → 7th century CE, when Xuanzang saw decline.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: The Bhimasena Jataka refers to "Andhrapatha" (the Andhra country) (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Bhavaviveka, a Madhyamika teacher, was an acharya in the Buddhist vihara at Dhanyakataka (Amaravati) (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Buddhist philosophers of Andhra: Aryadeva — Chittasuddhi Prakarana; Dignaga — Pramana Samucchaya (logic) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Sanchi and Bharhut stupas
events.summary: The great stupa at Sanchi (begun by Ashoka) gets stone railings and four carved gateways (toranas) in Shunga–Satavahana times (2nd–1st century BCE); Bharhut's railings show Jataka stories (NCERT).
events.detail:
A stupa is a mound over relics with a harmika and chhatri, surrounded by a railing (vedika) and a path for circling (pradakshina patha) (NCERT). The Sanchi gateways show the Buddha only through symbols — the empty seat, the wheel, the tree, footprints — and are carved like ivory (NCERT). An inscription says the ivory-workers of Vidisha carved one of them.

NCERT notes that Sanchi survived intact because the Begums of Bhopal (Shahjehan Begum and Sultan Jehan Begum) protected it; John Marshall later restored it. It was "discovered" in 1818 (NCERT).
outcomes: UNESCO World Heritage Site (1989).
facts: Sanchi was "discovered" in 1818 (NCERT).
Parts of a stupa: anda (hemispherical dome), harmika (railed box on top), chhatri (umbrella), yashti (mast), vedika (railing), torana (gateway), medhi (drum/terrace) (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"

events.title: Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati schools of sculpture
events.summary: Under the Kushanas and Satavahanas the Buddha is first shown in human form, in three styles: Gandhara (grey schist, Greek-Roman look), Mathura (red sandstone, Indian look) and Amaravati (white limestone, narrative panels) (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT notes that by the 1st century CE images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas were made at Mathura and Taxila. Gandhara images have wavy hair and robes like Roman togas; Mathura images are full and smiling and include Jaina and Hindu images; the Amaravati school shows crowded, lively scenes.

This period also saw Mahayana Buddhism, with Bodhisattvas as saviours (NCERT).
outcomes: Spread of Buddha images to Central Asia, China and Southeast Asia.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
facts: Gandhara art is Greco-Roman in style; Amaravati used white or greenish limestone (Palnadu marble).

events.title: Charaka and Sushruta: Ayurveda
events.summary: The Charaka Samhita (medicine) and the Sushruta Samhita (surgery) take shape in the early centuries CE — the foundations of Ayurveda.
events.detail: Charaka, by tradition the physician of Kanishka, described diagnosis and many drugs. Sushruta described over 100 surgical instruments, cataract surgery and rhinoplasty (rebuilding the nose). Vagbhata later wrote the Ashtanga Hridaya.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Bharata's Natyashastra
events.summary: Bharata Muni's Natyashastra (c. 200 BCE – 200 CE) lays down the rules of drama, dance and music and the theory of rasa (emotional flavour).
events.detail: It describes stage, costume, gestures (mudras), musical instruments and eight rasas such as shringara (love) and vira (heroism). All Indian classical dances, including Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam, trace their grammar to it.
outcomes: Basis of Indian classical dance and drama.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Panchatantra
events.summary: Vishnu Sharma's Panchatantra, animal fables teaching wise conduct, is composed in Sanskrit (c. 3rd century CE) and later travels across the world.
events.detail: It has five books. It was translated into Pahlavi (6th century), then Arabic as Kalila wa Dimna, and later into European languages. The Hitopadesha (Narayana) is a later version.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Tamil epics: Silappadikaram and Manimekalai
events.summary: The Tamil epics Silappadikaram, by Ilango Adigal, and Manimekalai, by Sittalai Sattanar, are composed (c. 5th–6th century CE) — two of the "five great epics" of Tamil.
events.detail: Silappadikaram tells of Kannagi, whose husband Kovalan is wrongly executed in Madurai; she burns the city in anger. Manimekalai, its sequel, tells of Kovalan's daughter, who becomes a Buddhist nun. The Tirukkural of Tiruvalluvar, on ethics, is older.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Thiruvalluvar wrote the Tirukkural; Tirutakkadevar wrote Jivaka Chintamani; Sithalai Sathanar wrote Manimekalai.

events.title: Gupta temples: Deogarh and Udayagiri
events.summary: Gupta-period temples begin stone temple architecture in the north: the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (c. 500 CE) has the first shikhara, and the Udayagiri caves (401 CE) show the great Varaha panel (NCERT shows Deogarh).
events.detail: Early temples were small square rooms (garbhagriha) with a porch; at Deogarh a tower (shikhara) rose above. Bhitargaon is a brick temple. Sanchi temple 17 is an early flat-roofed shrine. The Mehrauli iron pillar and Sarnath Buddha are other Gupta masterpieces (NCERT notes the Sarnath school).
outcomes: Nagara style of temple architecture developed from here.

participants.role: Udayagiri caves were made in his reign.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
facts: Panchayatan style: a main shrine with four smaller shrines at the corners (Dashavatara temple, Deogarh).

events.title: Elephanta caves
events.summary: The rock-cut Shiva cave on Elephanta island near Mumbai (c. 6th century, Kalachuri period) has the colossal three-headed Maheshamurti.
events.detail: The Portuguese named the island after a stone elephant. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Varahamihira's Brihatsamhita
events.summary: Varahamihira of Ujjain writes the Panchasiddhantika, summarising five schools of astronomy, and the Brihatsamhita, an encyclopaedia of astronomy, architecture, gems and more (6th century).
events.detail: He worked after Aryabhata. Brahmagupta (628) later gave rules for zero; Bhaskara II wrote the Lilavati (1150).

alsoOn.text: Bhaskara II writes the Siddhanta Shiromani, including the Lilavati.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: The Romaka Siddhanta (one of the five siddhantas in the Panchasiddhantika) deals with astronomy; the others are Paulisa, Paitamaha, Vasishtha and Surya (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Kalamalla: the first full Telugu inscription
events.summary: The Kalamalla inscription (Kadapa district, c. 575 CE) of the Renati Chola king Dhananjaya is the earliest known inscription written fully in Telugu.
events.detail:
Telugu words appear earlier in Prakrit inscriptions (Satavahana and Ikshvaku). The Renati Cholas of Renadu (Kadapa–Kurnool) issued the first Telugu records; Erragudipadu and others followed. The Telugu–Kannada script grew from the southern Brahmi of Bhattiprolu.

The Telugu language got "classical language" status in 2008.
outcomes: Telugu became a language of royal records.

alsoOn.text: Telugu and Kannada are declared classical languages.

events.yearHook: c. 575 CE → Nannaya c. 1050: 500 years from inscription to poetry.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Brahmagupta and zero
events.summary: Brahmagupta writes the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE), giving rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers.
events.detail: Indian mathematicians used the place-value system with zero; it spread through the Arabs to Europe as "Arabic numerals". Al-Khwarizmi later wrote on Indian numbers.
events.yearHook: 628 CE — six years before the Aihole inscription.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Mamallapuram: rathas and Arjuna's Penance
events.summary: Under Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) the Pallavas carve the five monolithic rathas and the great relief of Arjuna's Penance (Descent of the Ganga) at Mamallapuram (7th century).
events.detail: Mahendravarman I had begun rock-cut cave temples. Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) built the structural Shore Temple (c. 700) and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram. Mamallapuram is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984).
outcomes: Start of the Dravida style.

alsoOn.text: Rajasimha builds the Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Alvars and Nayanars: Tamil bhakti hymns
events.summary: The Tamil devotional hymns of the 12 Alvars (Vishnu) and 63 Nayanars (Shiva), sung between the 6th and 9th centuries, are compiled in the 10th century as the Nalayira Divya Prabandham and the Tevaram (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT: they travelled from place to place singing in Tamil, came from all castes, including "untouchables", and some were women, such as Andal (Alvar) and Karaikkal Ammaiyar (Nayanar). Nathamuni compiled the Prabandham; Nambi Andar Nambi compiled the Tevaram. The Divya Prabandham was called the "Tamil Veda" (NCERT).
outcomes: Basis of the bhakti movement (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 6 "Bhakti-Sufi Traditions"

events.title: Pampa and Kannada literature
events.summary: Pampa, born at Vemulavada in Telangana, writes Vikramarjuna Vijaya (941) at the court of the Vemulavada Chalukya Arikesari II; with Ponna and Ranna he is one of the "three gems" of Kannada.
events.detail: Earlier the Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha I wrote the Kavirajamarga. Pampa's brother Jinavallabha's Kurkyala inscription has three Telugu kanda verses — among the earliest Telugu poetry.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Khajuraho temples
events.summary: The Chandela kings build the temples of Khajuraho (c. 950–1050), the finest of the nagara style; the Kandariya Mahadeva is the largest (NCERT shows it).
events.detail: NCERT explains that Kandariya Mahadeva (999) was built by king Dhangadeva and that such temples had a garbhagriha, mandapa and a high shikhara. The temples show gods, dancers and daily life. UNESCO site (1986).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Dilwara Jain temples
events.summary: Vimala, minister of the Chaulukya (Solanki) king Bhima I, builds the marble Vimal Vasahi temple at Mount Abu (1031); Tejpal adds the Luna Vasahi (1230).
events.detail: The temples are famous for very fine marble carving of the ceilings. The Sun Temple at Modhera (1026) belongs to the same dynasty.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Jagannath temple, Puri
events.summary: The Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga builds the Jagannath temple at Puri (12th century), in the Kalinga style; his kingdom ran from the Ganga to the Godavari.
events.detail: Kalinga temples have a rekha deul (curved tower) and jagamohana (hall). The Lingaraja temple at Bhubaneswar (11th century) is another example. The Rath Yatra of Puri is world famous.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Hoysala temples: Belur and Halebidu
events.summary: Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana builds the Chennakeshava temple at Belur (1117); the Hoysaleshvara temple at Halebidu (Dwarasamudra) follows — star-shaped temples of soft soapstone with intricate carving.
events.detail: Hoysala temples stand on a raised star-shaped platform (jagati). Somanathapura (1268) is another. Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

participants.role: Converted him to Vaishnavism, by tradition.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Kalhana's Rajatarangini
events.summary: Kalhana writes the Rajatarangini ("river of kings", 1148–49), a verse history of Kashmir — the first true historical work in Sanskrit (NCERT notes it).
events.detail: He used inscriptions, documents, eyewitness accounts and earlier histories, and was often critical of rulers (NCERT). Queen Didda of Kashmir (980–1003), mentioned in NCERT, is part of this history.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda
events.summary: Jayadeva writes the Sanskrit Gita Govinda (12th century), songs on Radha and Krishna that shape later bhakti poetry, music and Odissi dance.
events.detail: The songs are sung daily at the Jagannath temple, Puri.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Palkuriki Somanatha and desi Telugu
events.summary: The Virashaiva poet Palkuriki Somanatha writes the Basava Puranam in dwipada metre and simple "desi" Telugu, breaking from Sanskritised "marga" poetry (12th–13th century).
events.detail: Before him, Nannechoda (Kumarasambhavam) used many native words. Somanatha spread Basavanna's teachings in Telugu. Gona Budda Reddy's Ranganatha Ramayanam later used the same dwipada metre.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Muinuddin Chishti settles at Ajmer
events.summary: Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti comes to India about 1192 and settles at Ajmer; the Chishti order becomes the most influential Sufi order in India (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT explains Sufism: the Sufis sought union with God through love, music (sama), and a master-disciple bond (pir–murid) in khanqahs. Chishti saints included Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi), Baba Farid (Ajodhan), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi) and Nasiruddin Chiragh-i Delhi (NCERT). Other orders: Suhrawardi (Bahauddin Zakariya, Multan), Qadiri and Naqshbandi. Akbar visited the Ajmer dargah 14 times (NCERT).
outcomes: Sufism spread Islam and syncretic culture (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1192 — the year of the Second Battle of Tarain.

participants.role: Founded the Chishti order in India (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 6 "Bhakti-Sufi Traditions"
facts: Chishti: Muinuddin, Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid, Nizamuddin Auliya, Gesudaraz (Gulbarga). Suhrawardi: Bahauddin Zakariya and Shaikh Sadruddin Arif (Multan). Rishi order: Shaikh Nuruddin Rishi (Kashmir) (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Qutb Minar and Indo-Islamic architecture
events.summary: Qutbuddin Aibak begins the Qutb Minar (c. 1199) and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in Delhi; Iltutmish completes the minar, and Alauddin Khalji adds the Alai Darwaza (1311) with the first true arch (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT explains that the arch and dome, the "arcuate" style, came with the Turks, replacing the "trabeate" post-and-beam style. The Qutb Minar, about 72.5 m high, was repaired by Firoz Shah Tughlaq. Iltutmish's tomb (1235) and Sultan Ghari are early tombs. Later: Tughlaqabad, the Lodi tombs, and the Gol Gumbaz of Bijapur. The Qutb complex is a UNESCO site (1993).
outcomes: Arch, dome and calligraphy entered Indian architecture (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Alauddin Khalji builds the Alai Darwaza, with the first true arch in India.

events.yearHook: Qutb Minar c. 1199 → completed under Iltutmish.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Kakatiya art: Ramappa, Thousand Pillars and Perini
events.summary: Recharla Rudra, general of Ganapati Deva, builds the Ramappa temple at Palampet (1213), famous for floating bricks, black-basalt bracket figures (madanikas) and dance sculptures; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
events.detail:
Kakatiya monuments: the Thousand Pillar temple (Hanamkonda, Rudradeva, 1163), Warangal fort with its four Kirti Toranas (gateways — now on the Telangana emblem), and great tanks such as Pakhala, Ramappa, Laknavaram and Ghanpur.

Jayapa Senani, Ganapati Deva's elephant commander, wrote the Nritta Ratnavali on dance; the warrior dance Perini Sivatandavam was revived from it in the 20th century by Nataraja Ramakrishna.
outcomes: First UNESCO World Heritage Site in Telangana (2021).

alsoOn.text: Ramappa temple declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Madhvacharya and Dvaita
events.summary: Madhvacharya of Udupi (1238–1317) teaches Dvaita — God (Vishnu) and the soul are eternally different — completing the three great schools: Advaita (Shankara), Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja) and Dvaita.
events.detail: He founded the Krishna matha at Udupi. Later Vaishnava teachers include Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita) and Vallabhacharya (Shuddhadvaita, Pushti marg).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Vyasaraja (Vyasatirtha), a Madhva saint, was guru of Krishnadevaraya and of Purandara Dasa.
Vallabhacharya propagated Pushtimarga, a religion of grace (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Konark Sun Temple
events.summary: The Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I builds the Sun Temple at Konark (c. 1250) as a giant stone chariot with 24 wheels pulled by 7 horses (NCERT shows the wheel).
events.detail: Europeans called it the "Black Pagoda". The wheel appears on the ₹10 note. UNESCO site (1984).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Jnaneshwar and the Marathi bhakti saints
events.summary: Jnaneshwar writes the Jnaneshwari (1290), a Marathi commentary on the Gita; with Namdev, Eknath and Tukaram he forms the Warkari tradition centred on Vitthala of Pandharpur (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT notes that these saints rejected ritual and caste and sang in Marathi; Sakhubai and the family of Chokhamela (who was of the "untouchable" Mahar caste) were among them. Tukaram (17th century) wrote abhangs.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Ranganatha Ramayanam
events.summary: Gona Budda Reddy, a Kakatiya feudatory, writes the Ranganatha Ramayanam (c. 1300) in dwipada — the first Telugu Ramayana, still used in Tholu Bommalata (leather puppet) shows.
events.detail: Its folk-style metre made it popular with performers. Later Telugu Ramayanas include the Bhaskara Ramayanam and the Molla Ramayanam.
events.yearHook: c. 1300 — last decades of the Kakatiyas.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Srinatha, "Kavi Sarvabhauma"
events.summary: Srinatha, court poet (Vidyadhikari) of Pedakomati Vema Reddi of Kondavidu, writes Sringara Naishadhamu, Kasi Khandamu, Haravilasamu and Palnati Viracharitra; at Deva Raya II's court he wins a debate and is bathed in gold coins (kanakabhishekam).
events.detail: His Chatuvulu (witty single verses) describe life across Andhra. He also translated Sriharsha's Naishadhiya Charita. He died poor after the Reddi kingdoms fell.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Srinatha wrote Haravilasam, Sivaratri Mahatmyam and Palnati Veera Charitra; Madanavilasabanam is NOT his (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Chaitanya and Purandara Dasa
events.summary: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (b. 1486) spreads Krishna bhakti in Bengal and Odisha through kirtan; Purandara Dasa (b. 1484) of Vijayanagara becomes the "father of Carnatic music".
events.detail: Other saints of this age: Sankaradeva in Assam (Ek Sarana dharma, namghars), Vallabhacharya, Surdas and Mirabai in the north (NCERT). Purandara Dasa composed thousands of Kannada songs and fixed graded lessons (sarali varase) still used in Carnatic music.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Hampi: the Vitthala and Hazara Rama temples
events.summary: Under Krishnadevaraya Vijayanagara builds grand temples with tall gateways (raya gopurams) and pillared halls — the Vitthala temple with its musical pillars and stone chariot, and the Hazara Rama temple (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT describes the royal centre: the Mahanavami Dibba (a platform for the nine-day festival), the Lotus Mahal and the elephant stables, and the sacred centre with the Virupaksha temple. Water came by canals from the Tungabhadra (NCERT). Colin Mackenzie surveyed the ruins in 1800 (NCERT). Lepakshi (Anantapur) and the Tadipatri temples are Vijayanagara works in Andhra.
outcomes: UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"

events.title: Krishnadevaraya's Ashtadiggajas
events.summary: Krishnadevaraya, himself author of the Telugu Amuktamalyada (NCERT), keeps eight great poets, the Ashtadiggajas, at his court Bhuvana Vijayam — the golden age of Telugu prabandha poetry.
events.detail:
The eight: Allasani Peddana (Manucharitra; "Andhra Kavita Pitamaha"), Nandi Thimmana (Parijatapaharanamu), Madayyagari Mallana, Dhurjati (Kalahasti Mahatmyam), Ayyalaraju Ramabhadrudu, Pingali Surana (Kalapurnodayam), Ramarajabhushanudu (Vasucharitra) and Tenali Ramakrishna (Panduranga Mahatmyam).

Krishnadevaraya said "Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa" — Telugu is the finest of the regional languages.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus); NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"
facts: Nandi Timmana; the courtyard of Vijayanagara temples had Kalyaana Mandapas (marriage halls).
Vemana Satakam is Vemana's verse collection.
Lepakshi has Vijayanagara Bhitti Chitras (wall paintings).

events.title: Molla Ramayanam
events.summary: Atukuri Molla, a woman poet from a potter family of Gopavaram (Kadapa), writes a short, simple Molla Ramayanam in the 16th century.
events.detail: She chose easy Telugu over heavy Sanskrit. Tarigonda Vengamamba (18th century) is another celebrated woman poet.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Women writers: Molla — Ramayanam; Tallapaka Timmakka (Annamacharya's wife) — Subhadra Kalyanam; Oduva Tirumalamba — Varadambika Parinayam; Gangadevi wrote Madhura Vijayam — pairing her with Marichi Parinayam is wrong (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Mughal painting: the Hamzanama
events.summary: Akbar's studio, led by the Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad, paints the giant Hamzanama (c. 1562–77); under Jahangir, Mansur and Abul Hasan perfect nature and portrait painting (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT notes that Mughal chronicles such as the Akbarnama were illustrated. Daswanth and Basawan were leading Indian painters at Akbar's court. Rajput and Pahari schools grew later (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes II, Ch. 9; NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II
facts: Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad from Iran (Safavid court) to Delhi; Jahangir's reign is the golden period of Mughal painting; European painting reached the court through the Portuguese Jesuits and English envoys, not Danish merchants (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Humayun's tomb and Fatehpur Sikri
events.summary: Humayun's tomb in Delhi (completed c. 1570), built by his widow, is the first great garden-tomb (char bagh) with a double dome; Akbar then builds Fatehpur Sikri (1571), with the Buland Darwaza (1575) (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT notes the char bagh garden and the "hasht bihisht" plan of Humayun's tomb, the model for the Taj Mahal. Fatehpur Sikri had the Jama Masjid, the tomb of Sheikh Salim Chishti, the Panch Mahal and the Ibadat Khana; it was abandoned after about 14 years. Shah Jahan's reign then gave the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort (1639–48) and the Jama Masjid of Delhi.
outcomes: Model for the Taj Mahal.

alsoOn.text: Akbar begins building Fatehpur Sikri (NCERT).
Shah Jahan begins the Red Fort at Shahjahanabad (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II
facts: Akbar's tomb is at Sikandara near Agra; Humayun's tomb at Delhi; Taj Mahal at Agra; Charminar at Hyderabad (APPSC Group-1 key).
Fatehpur Sikri has the Jami Masjid, Buland Darwaza and the tomb of Salim Chishti.

events.title: Tulsidas begins the Ramcharitmanas
events.summary: Tulsidas begins the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi (1574), the Ramayana of the Hindi heartland; Surdas's Sursagar (Braj) and Mirabai's bhajans belong to the same age (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT notes that bhakti saints wrote in regional languages that people understood. Mirabai, a Rajput princess, was a disciple of Ravidas, a leather-worker saint (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II

events.title: Qutb Shahi architecture: Mecca Masjid and the tombs
events.summary: The Qutb Shahis give Hyderabad its look: Golconda fort with its clapping-sound acoustics, the Charminar (1591), the Mecca Masjid (begun 1617), and the Qutb Shahi tombs on high platforms with onion domes.
events.detail: Their style mixed Persian, Pathan and local Hindu elements. They patronised Telugu (Ibrahim Qutb Shah as "Malki Bharama"), Persian and Dakhni Urdu (Muhammad Quli). Kuchipudi and Kshetrayya's padams also flourished under them. The Gol Gumbaz of Bijapur (1656), with one of the world's largest domes and a whispering gallery, is the Adil Shahi counterpart.

alsoOn.text: Gol Gumbaz of Muhammad Adil Shah completed at Bijapur.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Kshetrayya's padams and Kuchipudi
events.summary: Kshetrayya of Movva composes Telugu padams on Muvva Gopala for dancers at Madurai, Tanjore and Golconda; Siddhendra Yogi shapes Kuchipudi with Bhama Kalapam (17th century, by tradition).
events.detail: Telugu was the court language of the Nayaks of Madurai and Tanjore, where Telugu literature flourished (the "southern school"). Kshetrayya's padams are still danced in Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Vemana, the people's poet
events.summary: Vemana, the "praja kavi", writes simple Telugu verses (ataveladi metre) mocking caste, idol worship and hypocrisy; C.P. Brown collects and translates them into English (1829). The syllabus names him under "Praja Kavi".
events.detail: His dates are uncertain — usually placed in the 17th century, in Rayalaseema. Each verse ends "Vishwadabhirama vinura vema". Brown called him the poet of the people.

alsoOn.text: C.P. Brown publishes Vemana's verses with an English translation.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Tarigonda Vengamamba and Tirumala annadanam
events.summary: Tarigonda Vengamamba (1730–1817), a widowed poet and devotee of Venkateswara, writes Telugu works and starts free food for pilgrims at Tirumala.
events.detail: She defied the customs forced on widows. TTD's free meal scheme is named after her.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Poets of the 18th century and their languages: Tayumanavar — Tamil; Warris (Waris) Shah — Punjabi (Heer Ranjha); Kunchan Nambiar — Malayalam (Ottan Thullal); Dayaram — Gujarati (not Marathi) (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Tyagaraja and the Carnatic Trinity
events.summary: Tyagaraja (born 1767) composes thousands of Telugu kritis at Tiruvaiyaru; with Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri he forms the Trinity of Carnatic music.
events.detail: Most of the Trinity's songs are in Telugu, the court language of the Tanjore Marathas and Nayaks. The Tyagaraja Aradhana at Tiruvaiyaru is held every year. Earlier, Annamacharya and Purandara Dasa had laid the base.
events.yearHook: Born 1767 — same decade as Buxar's aftermath.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Tyagaraja (Thyagaraya) is regarded as the pioneer composer of the kriti form of Carnatic music; Annamacharya was the pioneer of the sankirtana/pada form; Purandaradasa is the "father of Carnatic music" (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Colin Mackenzie's survey and the kaifiyats
events.summary: Colin Mackenzie surveys the ruins of Hampi (1800) (NCERT) and, with his Telugu assistants the Kavali brothers (Boriah, Lakshmaiah), collects thousands of village histories (kaifiyats), inscriptions and palm-leaf manuscripts of south India.
events.detail: NCERT notes that Mackenzie, a surveyor and antiquarian, prepared the first survey map of Hampi and gathered local traditions. He became the first Surveyor General of India (1815). His collection is a major source for Andhra history; the syllabus names him in "Socio-Cultural, Literary Awakening".
outcomes: Mackenzie manuscripts preserved at Chennai.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes II, Ch. 7; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Christian missionaries in Andhra
events.summary: The London Missionary Society opens a mission at Visakhapatnam (1805); missionaries translate the Bible into Telugu, set up schools, hospitals and printing presses, and work among Dalits and women.
events.detail:
Missions spread: the American Lutherans under J.C.F. Heyer at Guntur (1842), Anglicans at Machilipatnam where Robert Noble founded the Noble College (1843), Baptists at Nellore and Ongole, and the Godavari Delta Mission. Mass movements of Dalit conversion occurred in the 1870s.

The syllabus asks about the "Role of Christian Missionaries": they spread modern education and printing in Telugu, but also provoked reform within Hindu society (Veeresalingam).
outcomes: Telugu printing and schools; Noble College (1843); Dalit education.

alsoOn.text: J.C.F. Heyer starts the American Lutheran mission at Guntur.
Robert Noble opens a school at Machilipatnam — later Noble College.

participants.role: Hindu reformer partly responding to missionaries.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Benjamin Schultze, a Danish-Halle (German) missionary, first translated the Bible into Telugu (1746-47) (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: C.P. Brown and the Telugu revival
events.summary: C.P. Brown publishes Vemana's verses with an English translation (1829), collects and edits old Telugu texts, and writes a Telugu grammar (1840) and a Telugu–English dictionary (1852).
events.detail: Brown came to Madras in 1817 and learnt Telugu at Kadapa. He spent his own money to employ pandits to copy and correct manuscripts of the Mahabharata, Bhagavatam and Vasucharitra, ran free schools at Machilipatnam and Kadapa, and printed Telugu books. He is called the father of the modern revival of Telugu literature.
outcomes: Classical Telugu works saved and printed.

alsoOn.text: C.P. Brown publishes his Telugu–English dictionary.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Raja Ravi Varma
events.summary: Raja Ravi Varma of Travancore wins a prize at the Madras exhibition (1873) and becomes the most famous Indian painter, using European oils for Indian myths; his press (1894) made cheap prints for every home.
events.detail: His Shakuntala and Damayanti became popular images. The Bengal School (1905) later reacted against his European style.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Narayana Guru at Aruvippuram
events.summary: Narayana Guru, a reformer of the Ezhava community of Kerala, consecrates a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram (1888), defying the rule that only Brahmins could; the SNDP Yogam (1903) carries on his work. The syllabus names him with Phule and Periyar.
events.detail: His message was "one caste, one religion, one God for man". He set up temples, schools and associations open to all castes. The Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–25) for the right to use temple roads drew on his movement.
outcomes: SNDP Yogam (1903); Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–25).

alsoOn.text: Sri Narayana Dharma Paripalana (SNDP) Yogam founded.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25, Travancore) was for the right of avarnas to use roads around the Vaikom temple; led by T. K. Madhavan, K. P. Kesava Menon, supported by Gandhi and E. V. Ramasamy (called Vaikom Veerar) (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu and the Brahmo movement
events.summary: Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu leads the Brahmo Samaj and the social purity (anti-nautch) movement in Andhra from the 1890s, working for women's education, widow remarriage and against untouchability.
events.detail: He taught at Machilipatnam and Hyderabad and was principal of the Pithapuram Raja's College, Kakinada (from 1905), which became a centre of reform. With Veeresalingam he shaped Telugu social reform. He became Vice-Chancellor of Madras University (1925).
outcomes: Brahmo ideals spread in coastal Andhra.
events.yearHook: 1890s, between Veeresalingam (1881) and the 1905 Swadeshi wave.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu was mainly responsible for ending the "Bhogam" (nautch) system (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

events.title: Bengal School: Bharat Mata
events.summary: Abanindranath Tagore paints "Bharat Mata" (1905), the image of the Swadeshi movement, founding the Bengal School, which rejected European academic art for Indian and Asian styles.
events.detail: E.B. Havell and Nandalal Bose were part of it. Rabindranath Tagore's Santiniketan (Visva-Bharati, 1921) became a centre of art education.

alsoOn.text: Rabindranath Tagore founds Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: The Indian Society of Oriental Art (Calcutta, 1907) was founded by Abanindranath Tagore with Gaganendranath Tagore to revive ancient Indian art traditions (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Telugu press: Krishna Patrika and Andhra Patrika
events.summary: Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao starts the Andhra Patrika (Bombay, 1908; a daily from Madras, 1914); with the Krishna Patrika (Machilipatnam, 1902, edited by Mutnuri Krishna Rao) it spreads nationalism in Telugu. Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao is jailed for sedition in 1908.
events.detail: Earlier came missionary papers and Veeresalingam's Vivekavardhini (1874). The press carried the Vandemataram and Non-Cooperation messages to villages. The syllabus asks for the "Role of News Paper".
outcomes: Telugu political journalism.

alsoOn.text: Krishna Patrika begins at Machilipatnam.
Veeresalingam starts the journal Vivekavardhini.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Andhra Prakasika was edited by A.P. Parthasarathi Naidu — pairing it with P. Ananda Charlu is wrong (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

Veeresalingam is the father of the renaissance in Andhra; Andhra Patrika was the first Telugu political newsweekly; Krishna Patrika was started in 1902 by Konda Venkatappayya; "The Crescent" (English weekly) was founded by Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty, not Mutnuri Krishna Rao (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
The 2025 key treats Krishna Patrika as the first Telugu newspaper (older journals such as Satyadoota, 1835, were missionary papers) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Veeresalingam founded Vivekavardhini; he also opened the first girls' schools at Rajahmundry (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Gidugu Ramamurthy and spoken Telugu
events.summary: Gidugu Ramamurthy leads the vyavaharika (spoken-language) movement for writing and teaching in everyday Telugu instead of classical grandhika Telugu (from about 1910); his birthday, 29 August, is Telugu Language Day.
events.detail: With Gurajada Apparao, who wrote Kanyasulkam in spoken Telugu, he fought the purists who controlled school texts. He also created a script, grammar and books for the Savara tribal language. The movement won by the 1930s–40s.
outcomes: Modern Telugu prose and schooling in spoken Telugu.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Indian and Telugu cinema begin
events.summary: Dadasaheb Phalke releases Raja Harishchandra (1913), India's first feature film; Telugu cinema follows with the silent Bhishma Pratigna (1921) and the first Telugu talkie, H.M. Reddy's Bhakta Prahlada (1931).
events.detail: Raghupathi Venkaiah Naidu, who built the first cinema halls in Madras, is called the father of Telugu cinema. Alam Ara (1931) was the first Indian talkie. Telugu winners of the Dadasaheb Phalke Award: B.N. Reddi (1974), L.V. Prasad (1982), Akkineni Nageswara Rao (1990), D. Ramanaidu (2009) and K. Viswanath (2016).

alsoOn.text: Bhakta Prahlada, the first Telugu talkie (H.M. Reddy); Alam Ara, the first Indian talkie.
Bhishma Pratigna, the first Telugu silent feature film.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Bhava kavitvam: Telugu romantic poetry
events.summary: Rayaprolu Subbarao's Trinakankanam (1913) begins "bhava kavitvam", Telugu romantic poetry of love, nature and patriotism; Devulapalli Krishna Sastri and others follow.
events.detail: Rayaprolu also wrote the patriotic song "Ye desamegina endu kalidina, pogadara nee talli bhoomi Bharatini". The movement gave way in the 1930s–40s to progressive (abhyudaya) poetry led by Sri Sri.
events.yearHook: 1913 — year of the first Andhra Mahasabha.

participants.role: Led the progressive poetry that followed.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)

events.title: Andhra library movement
events.summary: Ayyanki Venkataramanaiah founds the Andhra Desa Grandhalaya Sangham at Vijayawada (1914), with Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao, and the journal Grandhalaya Sarvasvamu (1915); libraries spread to villages as centres of adult education and nationalism.
events.detail:
Early libraries included the Saraswathi Nilayam and the Rammohan Library (Vijayawada). Libraries ran night schools, reading rooms and lectures; they were key to the national movement in Andhra. The Madras Public Libraries Act (1948) was the first library law in India; Andhra Pradesh passed its own in 1960.

The syllabus lists the "Library Movement" and names Ayyanki Venkataratnam and Gadicherla.
outcomes: Madras Public Libraries Act (1948), India's first.

alsoOn.text: Madras Public Libraries Act — the first library law in India.

events.yearHook: 1914 — a year after the Andhra Mahasabha.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Libraries: Sri Krishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam — Hyderabad, 1901; Vignana Chandrika Granthamandali — Hyderabad, 1906; Andhra Saraswati Parishad — Kovvur, 1916; Andhra Council of Research — Hyderabad, 1922 (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Grandhalaya Sarvasvam (Telugu) began in 1915; Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao started "boat library" services in West Godavari (1918) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao wrote his autobiography "Na Jeevitha Katha"; Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Choudary was called "Kavi Raju"; Duggirala Gopalakrishnaiah raised the "Rama Dandu"; Parvataneni Veeraiah Choudary led the Pedanandipadu agitation (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Women of Andhra: Dokka Seethamma and Ponaka Kanakamma
events.summary: Ponaka Kanakamma founds the Sujanaranjani Samajam at Nellore (1913) and later the Kasturba Devi girls' school; Dokka Seethamma (died 1909) is remembered for feeding all who came to her door. The syllabus names both under "Role of women".
events.detail: Other women of the movement: Duvvuri Subbamma (first woman of Andhra jailed in Non-Cooperation), Durgabai Deshmukh (Andhra Mahila Sabha, 1937) and Unnava Lakshmi Bayamma.

alsoOn.text: Durgabai Deshmukh founds the Andhra Mahila Sabha in Madras.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
outcomes: Women joined the national movement in large numbers in Andhra.
Andhra Mahila Sabha (1937) spread women's education.

events.title: Justice Party and the non-Brahmin movement
events.summary: T.M. Nair and Theagaraya Chetty found the South Indian Liberal Federation — the Justice Party — (November 1916) and issue the Non-Brahmin Manifesto; it wins the 1920 elections, and the Raja of Panagal (1921–26) issues the first Communal G.O. on reservation.
events.detail:
The party wanted more jobs and education for non-Brahmins and cooperated with the British reforms of 1919. Its ministries set up Andhra University (1926), passed the Hindu Religious Endowments Act and gave women the vote in the province (1921). Many leaders were Telugu zamindars and landlords.

The Self-Respect Movement of Periyar (1925) carried the non-Brahmin cause forward; the Justice Party merged into Periyar's Dravidar Kazhagam (1944).
outcomes: Communal G.O. (1921); Andhra University (1926); Dravidar Kazhagam (1944).

alsoOn.text: Justice Party wins the first elections under the 1919 Act in Madras.
Raja of Panagal becomes Chief Minister; first Communal G.O.
Justice Party becomes the Dravidar Kazhagam under Periyar.

events.yearHook: 1916 — the year of the Lucknow Pact.
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
facts: The Justice Party government helped found Andhra University (1926) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Nationalist literature: Garimella and Unnava
events.summary: During Non-Cooperation Garimella Satyanarayana's song "Maa kodi tella doratanamu" (1921) is sung across Andhra and he is jailed; Unnava Lakshminarayana's novel Malapalli (1922), on Dalit and peasant life, is banned by the British.
events.detail: The syllabus lists "Nationalist and Revolutionary Literature". Others: Chilakamarthi Lakshmi Narasimham's poem on the 1907 Kakinada events ("Bharata khandambu chakkani padi aavu"), Rayaprolu's patriotic songs, and Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary's rationalist works (Sambuka Vadha, Kurukshetra Sangramamu) of the 1920s.
outcomes: Telugu literature became a weapon of the national movement.

alsoOn.text: Unnava Lakshminarayana's Malapalli published; later banned.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Kodali Anjaneyulu's drama "Viplava Parivartanamu" was banned during Non-Cooperation (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
The lyric "Veera gandhamu techinaramu, veerulevvaro telpudi" was sung during the Salt Satyagraha (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

Salt Satyagraha in Andhra (1930): Bulusu Sambamurty broke the salt law at Kakinada, Dandu Narayana Raju at Mattapalem, Kasi Viswanadham at Vadarevu, Pattabhi Sitaramayya at Masulipatnam (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Gurajada's song "Desamante matti kadoi, desamante manushuloi" is in his collection Mutyala Saralu (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramaiah founded Andhra Bank (Machilipatnam, 1923) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Gurram Jashuva's Gabbilam and Dalit voices
events.summary: Gurram Jashuva writes Gabbilam ("the bat", 1941): an untouchable sends a message to Lord Shiva through a bat, since he himself may not enter the temple. With Boyi Bheemanna, he gives Dalits a strong voice in Telugu poetry.
events.detail: Jashuva, from Vinukonda, faced caste and religious discrimination; he also wrote Firdausi and Kandiseekudu. Boyi Bheemanna wrote the play Palerugadu (1940s) and Gudiselu Kalipotunnai (Sahitya Akademi 1975). The syllabus names both.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Gurram Jashuva: born 28 September; called "Poet of the Millennium"; Sahitya Akademi Award 1964 for Kreestu Charitra (not Gabbilam); member of the AP Legislative Council (1964); Padma Bhushan (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Rayaprolu Subbarao is called "Abhinava Nannaya" (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Praja Natya Mandali and Burrakatha
events.summary: The Praja Natya Mandali (1943), the Andhra wing of the Indian People's Theatre Association, uses folk forms such as Burrakatha — made famous by Shaik Nazar — to carry political messages to villages.
events.detail: Andhra folk and tribal forms in the syllabus include Burrakatha (ballad with tambura and drums), Harikatha, Tholu Bommalata (leather puppets), Yakshaganam (Veedhi Natakam), Oggu Katha, Chindu Bhagavatam, the Lambadi and Koya dances, and the Dhimsa dance of the Araku tribes. The play "Maa Bhoomi" (1947) supported the Telangana struggle.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Festivals and folk arts of Andhra: Sankranti (Makara Sankranti, with Gangireddulu, Haridasu and kites), Ugadi, Bathukamma (Telangana), Sammakka-Saralamma jatara (Medaram, Telangana); dances Kolattam, Dappu, Tappeta Gullu, Veeranatyam (dance of warriors), Butta Bommalu, Gobbi; Banjara (Lambadi) dances.
Crafts: Budithi brassware (Srikakulam), Durgi stone carving (Palnadu), Etikoppaka lacquer toys, Kondapalli toys.

events.title: National anthem, song and emblem adopted
events.summary: On 24 January 1950 the Constituent Assembly adopts Tagore's "Jana Gana Mana" as the national anthem and Bankim Chandra's "Vande Mataram" as the national song; the Sarnath lion capital becomes the state emblem on 26 January 1950.
events.detail: The national flag (designed from Pingali Venkayya's flag) was adopted on 22 July 1947. The national calendar (Saka era) was adopted in 1957. "Satyameva Jayate" from the Mundaka Upanishad is under the emblem.

alsoOn.text: The Constituent Assembly adopts the national flag (22 July 1947).

events.yearHook: 24 January 1950 — two days before the Republic.

participants.role: His design led to the flag.
The emblem is his Sarnath capital.

events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)

events.title: Sri Sri's Maha Prasthanam
events.summary: Sri Sri's Maha Prasthanam (poems from 1934, published 1950) begins progressive (abhyudaya) Telugu poetry for workers and the poor; he later leads the revolutionary writers' association Virasam (1970).
events.detail: The Abhyudaya Rachayitala Sangham (Arasam, 1943) brought progressive writers together. Famous line: "Maro prapancham, maro prapancham pilichindi".
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Books and authors: Japaneeyamu — Sriram Veerabrahmam; Mahaprasthanam — Sri Sri; Kanyasulkam — Gurajada Appa Rao; Veyipadagalu — Viswanatha Satyanarayana (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: National academies of the arts
events.summary: The Sahitya Akademi (letters) and Lalit Kala Akademi (fine arts) are set up in 1954, after the Sangeet Natak Akademi (music, dance, drama, 1953); the National School of Drama follows in 1959.
events.detail: Maulana Azad, as Education Minister, guided their creation. The Sahitya Akademi gives awards in 24 languages.

events.title: Jnanpith for Telugu: Viswanatha Satyanarayana
events.summary: Viswanatha Satyanarayana wins the first Jnanpith Award for Telugu (1970) for Ramayana Kalpavrukshamu; C. Narayana Reddy (1988, Viswambhara) and Ravuri Bharadwaja (2012, Paakudu Raallu) follow.
events.detail: The Jnanpith began in 1965 (G. Sankara Kurup, Malayalam). Viswanatha's novel Veyipadagalu was translated into Hindi as Sahasraphan by P.V. Narasimha Rao.

alsoOn.text: C. Narayana Reddy wins the Jnanpith for Viswambhara.
Ravuri Bharadwaja wins the Jnanpith for Paakudu Raallu.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
facts: Viswanatha Satyanarayana was the first Telugu writer to win the Jnanpith, for Ramayana Kalpavruksham (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
